title: HACCP for restaurateurs: three pages that protect your business
excerpt: Process maps, hazards, CCPs, and critical limits: put together a working HACCP plan in a week. A day-by-day route instead of a folder kept “just in case.”

body.text: In many restaurant chains, the HACCP plan sits in an accounting office in a folder marked “just in case.” In a good restaurant, it is a working document that people actually use to track hazards. You can put one together in a week if you keep it practical.
Draw every stage on one sheet: receiving → storage → preparation → heat treatment → serving → cleaning. Do not worry about using pencil and drawing by hand; you can prepare a clean copy later.

At each stage, note what could go wrong. Biological (salmonella on chicken), chemical (detergent residue after washing), and physical (a glass fragment in a dessert). Assess the likelihood and severity—subjectively, but honestly.

items: Choose 3–6 points where a hazard can be eliminated or controlled.
Set a limit: “chicken core ≥ 75 °C for 5 minutes.”
Decide who will measure it and how.
Define what to do if the limit is exceeded.

body.text: Link every CCP to a specific log: temperatures go in the temperature log, finished-product checks in their log, and cleaning in the cleaning log. Do not create separate “HACCP logs”—they will drift out of sync.
Show the plan to the shift team, ask them to use it for one or two days, collect feedback, make revisions, and get the manager's signature. That is it: the basic HACCP plan is ready.

body.title: Review it after a month
body.text: A HACCP plan is not set in stone. After 30 days, the team may sit down and rewrite half the items—that is normal and how the plan becomes useful in practice.
